stories.body: France is preparing for a second day of nationwide protests following severe unrest a week earlier, with the Interior Ministry deploying 70,000 police and security personnel and imposing broad restrictions on demonstrations. President Emmanuel Macron has limited permitted protests to those organized by recognized unions, while several cities have imposed additional bans or curfews. In Paris, museums including the Louvre will close, a PSG match has been postponed, and businesses have boarded windows amid fears of renewed violence. Student groups, labor organizations and revived Yellow Vest activists are nevertheless expected to mobilize in large numbers.
stories.headline: France deploys 70,000 security personnel before new protests

stories.body: French anti-terrorism prosecutors are investigating a drive-by shooting in Trappes and nearby La Verrière, west of Paris, that killed one person and wounded five others, including a 12-year-old girl who was seriously injured. President Emmanuel Macron called it a racist terrorist attack, saying victims appeared to have been targeted because of their skin color or religion. Authorities arrested a 39-year-old suspect after he allegedly fired from a car at a petrol station, medical center and playground over roughly 15 minutes; the motive remains under investigation.
stories.headline: France investigates deadly shooting near Paris as suspected racist terrorist attack

stories.body: Seven people were killed and at least 34 others wounded when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Hmoud, in Jordan's Karak governorate. Witnesses described panic as worshippers sought cover beneath pews and fled while the shooting continued. The attackers escaped and no group has claimed responsibility, but Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya described them as extremists and King Abdullah II pledged the harshest penalties. Jordan declared three days of national mourning as security forces searched for those responsible.
stories.headline: Seven killed in gun attack at church funeral in Jordan

stories.body: Israel has imposed a closure on the occupied West Bank, launched raids across multiple towns and begun demolitions in and around Hebron after two Israeli soldiers were killed and three wounded in a shooting at a checkpoint near the city. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel would demolish the attackers' home area and was preparing for extensive action in the West Bank. Israeli ministers have called for forced displacement and a broader campaign, while rights advocates and Palestinian officials describe the measures as collective punishment. Israel's High Court temporarily halted some demolitions after an urgent petition.
stories.headline: Israel begins Hebron demolitions and West Bank raids after soldiers are killed

stories.body: Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan's northeast coast after briefly reaching super-typhoon strength, killing one person, injuring more than 500 and cutting power to more than 167,000 homes. Thousands of people were evacuated, much of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, remained closed for a second day, and hundreds of flights were cancelled. The storm, which previously had winds approaching 300 kilometers per hour, has weakened but is forecast to move toward China's east coast and southern Japan, bringing heavy rain and strong winds.
stories.headline: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures hundreds in Taiwan

stories.body: Kenya has recorded its second Ebola death in the country's first known outbreak, after a 65-year-old woman who was a close relative of the first victim died while in quarantine. Seven other patients, including relatives, health workers and a hospital cleaner, are being treated in isolation. The Health Ministry says all known cases belong to one cluster and that there is no evidence of community spread, but Kenya has tightened screening for travelers from the Democratic Republic of Congo and other high-risk countries as neighboring states remain on alert.
stories.headline: Kenya records a second Ebola death

stories.body: Internal polling from both parties indicates that several closely contested House races are tightening as Republicans pour money into defending seats, prompting some Democrats to lower expectations for the size of a potential majority. GOP candidates have reportedly narrowed races in the Midwest and Colorado and are working to stabilize vulnerable Florida districts, though Republicans remain under pressure in Texas and North Carolina. Democratic leaders still expect to win the House, but both parties now see many of the key contests as within the margin of error.
stories.headline: House battlegrounds tighten as Republicans defend vulnerable seats

stories.body: A new Politico poll finds that nearly half of Democratic midterm voters say they are voting mainly to oppose President Donald Trump, compared with 38% of Republican voters who say they are voting chiefly to support him. Almost half of Republican respondents instead said their main motivation was backing a local candidate, and many said candidates should be able to break with Trump where necessary to win. The findings point to a difficult balance for Republican candidates in competitive races as voter concerns about the cost of living, tariffs and the Iran war shape the campaign.
stories.headline: Poll finds Trump is motivating more Democratic opponents than Republican supporters

stories.body: New York City Council member Joann Ariola is pursuing legislation that would provide 911 callers with personalized, real-time updates on the location and expected arrival of ambulances. The proposal follows a comptroller's report showing that average ambulance response times for life-threatening emergencies have risen to 13 minutes, up more than 40% over a decade. Supporters say better information could help callers decide whether to seek other transportation, but city officials and EMS unions say the underlying problem is staff retention and low pay for EMTs and paramedics.
stories.headline: New York proposal would give 911 callers real-time ambulance updates

stories.body: Spain's Supreme Court has given the government until October 28 to provide the names of 163,020 people whose voting rights were provisionally suspended after they obtained nationality under the Democratic Memory Law, often called the grandchildren's law. The court warned the justice and foreign ministers of possible fines and further legal consequences for noncompliance. The dispute concerns the eligibility of overseas voters ahead of the November 29 general election; officials say that of more than 31,000 files reviewed, only 91 people have so far received certificates establishing the required connection to Spanish exile.
stories.headline: Spain's Supreme Court gives government five days to identify voters affected by suspension

stories.body: People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo has said he is prepared to complete a parliamentary majority with Vox after Spain's November election, making the removal of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez his primary objective. He also said he would eliminate the Equality Ministry as a standalone department, seek changes to the euthanasia law and reopen debate over whether 16- and 17-year-olds should be able to obtain abortions without parental knowledge. Feijóo's comments mark a departure from his earlier emphasis that the most-voted party should govern.
stories.headline: Feijóo signals willingness to rely on Vox to form a majority

stories.body: Prosecutors at Spain's National Court have concluded that Iran was behind the 2023 shooting of former European Parliament vice-president Alejo Vidal-Quadras in Madrid, according to their indictment against seven defendants. Prosecutors are seeking up to 27 years in prison for the alleged gunman and accuse others of providing logistical, financial and surveillance support. The filing says Vidal-Quadras, a founder of Vox and longtime critic of Tehran who supported Iranian opposition groups, had become a target of Iranian covert operations against dissidents abroad.
stories.headline: Spanish prosecutors conclude Iran was behind attempted assassination of Alejo Vidal-Quadras

stories.body: Spain's National Court has dismissed terrorism proceedings against 12 members of the Committees for the Defense of the Republic, or CDR, under the country's amnesty law. The ruling follows a July decision by the Court of Justice of the European Union that the law could apply to the case because the alleged acts did not intentionally cause serious human-rights violations. Prosecutors had sought prison sentences of between eight and 27 years over allegations involving a purported violent cell, explosives and planned attacks; the activists and their lawyers say the case should never have been brought.
stories.headline: National Court grants amnesty to 12 Catalan independence activists

stories.body: Mossos d'Esquadra evicted housing activists from a building on Carrer de Calàbria in Barcelona's Eixample district just hours after they occupied it. Police acted after the owner filed a complaint and treated the occupation as a flagrant offense; authorities reported confrontations during the operation and 19 people were cited for disobedience and resisting officers. The activists, linked to the Plaça de Catalunya housing encampment and local housing unions, had planned to use the six-floor building, which they said had been vacant for years, to house people without shelter.
stories.headline: Barcelona police evict housing activists from occupied Eixample building

stories.body: Barcelona City Council has started proceedings to close a recently opened supermarket in the former Ona bookshop on Gran de Gràcia after an inspection found it lacked an activity license and had undergone unpermitted construction work. The closure will not be immediate, but the district says it is pursuing an order to stop the business. The opening drew political criticism because the historic Catalan-language bookshop was a neighborhood cultural landmark, and the city is also enforcing a suspension of licenses for 24-hour supermarkets.
stories.headline: Barcelona moves to close unlicensed supermarket in former Ona bookshop

stories.body: More than 600 scientists have called for urgent preparations for a possible exceptionally strong El Niño event within eight months, warning that a Super El Niño could intensify heatwaves, torrential rain, storms and food-price pressures. Researchers say the event could temporarily push global warming close to 2°C above preindustrial levels, on top of already unusually warm oceans and atmosphere. For Catalonia and the Mediterranean, a warmer sea could increase the risk of severe weather including destructive DANA systems, while disrupted harvests elsewhere could affect global food supplies.
stories.headline: Scientists urge Catalonia to prepare for a possible Super El Niño
